title: Orbital Control of Reticulofenestra (Calcareous Nannofossils) Assemblages During the Early Pliocene
content:
Abstract

Orbital changes have shaped Earth's climate system and influenced the evolution and spatial distribution of marine plankton, including coccolithophores. Some studies have assessed eccentricity's impact on the diversity and morphological evolution of Noelaerhabdaceae taxa during the Quaternary. However, the response of pre-Pleistocene Noelaerhabdaceae species remains largely unexplored. Here, we examine how the extinct group Reticulofenestra, a dominant pre-Quaternary Noelaerhabdaceae taxon, responded to eccentricity during the Early Pliocene. This interval, characterized by relatively stable climate, offers a unique opportunity to investigate how orbital variations may have influenced coccolithophore morphological evolution. We analyzed sediments retrieved from the SW Iberian Margin (International Ocean Discovery Program 397 Expedition, Site U1587), a region with high sediment accumulation rates where astronomically forced climate mechanisms strongly influenced sedimentation. Calcareous nannofossil data show co-occurring high abundances of Reticulofenestra <3 μm and Reticulofenestra >7 μm, with open and closed central areas, during 400-kyr eccentricity minima. However, medium size Reticulofenestra morphotypes exhibit a gradual decline throughout the interval, punctuated by several abrupt decreases coinciding with 400-kyr eccentricity minima. We suggest that during these minima, reduced seasonality in daylight hours favored more stable conditions for K-strategist coccolithophores (Reticulofenestra <3 μm), allowing them to dominate the ecological niche and displace less resilient groups (medium size Reticulofenestra). However, the gradual decrease in Reticulofenestra size observed throughout the Early Pliocene could also reflect an adaptive response to improve nutrient assimilation under decreasing CO2 concentrations. Synchronous Reticulofenestra size reduction at 4.45 Ma in Agulhas Plateau (Southwest Indian Ocean) records suggests a large-scale teleconnection in nannofossil community dynamics.
